lessons.title: Fiscal Policy Refresher: How the Union Budget Moves Markets

body.text: The Union Budget is not an accounting statement. It is the single most market moving policy event on the Indian calendar, and every serious fund manager reads it for what it signals, not just what it spends.

children.text: Why Fund Managers Clear Their Calendar for Budget Day

Once a year, usually on February 1, the Finance Minister presents the Union Budget in Parliament under Article 112 of the Constitution. On paper, it is a statement of the government's expected receipts and expenditure for the coming financial year. In practice, it is the clearest window you get into how the government intends to tax, spend and borrow, and each of those three decisions moves a different part of the market.

This lesson treats the Budget as what it actually is for an investor: a policy document with five numbers that matter more than the rest, a borrowing programme that bond markets price within minutes, and a spending mix that decides which sectors get a tailwind for the next twelve months.
The Five Numbers That Move Markets on Budget Day
Strip away the political commentary, and every Budget boils down to five figures that traders and fund managers track in real time as the Finance Minister speaks.

body.caption: What to track on Budget day

cells: How much the government plans to borrow relative to GDP
The actual rupee amount of government bonds hitting the market
How much goes into roads, railways, defence and infrastructure versus subsidies
Changes to income tax slabs, customs duty and capital gains rules
How much the government expects to raise selling stakes in PSUs

body.label: FY26 fiscal deficit target
body.context: Down from a Covid-year peak of roughly 9.2% of GDP in FY21, as the government has stuck to a stated glide path back toward fiscal consolidation.

body.title: India's fiscal deficit as % of GDP (FY20-FY26)

body.text: Notice the shape of this trend before you read a single line of the Budget speech. A government on a credible fiscal consolidation path tends to get rewarded with softer bond yields even before it spends a rupee, simply because it is borrowing less than feared.

children.text: The Borrowing Programme: Where the Bond Market Gets Its Cue

markDefs.definition: Government Securities: bonds issued by the Government of India to fund its borrowing, traded on the wholesale debt market and treated as the risk-free benchmark for Indian interest rates.

children.text: The fiscal deficit has to be funded from somewhere, and in India that mostly means the government borrows by issuing government securities, or
G-Secs

, dated bonds sold at scheduled auctions through the year. The Budget announces the gross and net market borrowing figures for the coming year, and this single number, more than almost anything else in the speech, decides which way the 10-year G-Sec yield moves on Budget day.

markDefs.definition: Statutory Liquidity Ratio: the minimum share of a bank's net demand and time liabilities that must be held in approved securities, mostly government bonds, set by the RBI.

children.text: Banks are structurally large buyers of G-Secs because regulation requires them to hold a minimum share of deposits in approved government securities, a rule called the
Statutory Liquidity Ratio, or SLR

. When the government's borrowing programme comes in higher than the market expected, banks and insurers have to absorb more bond supply than they had planned for, bond prices fall, and yields rise. That single Budget day number can move the 10-year G-Sec yield by 10 to 20 basis points within the hour, and everything from home loan rates to corporate bond spreads eventually follows that benchmark.

body.title: Reading a Borrowing Surprise
body.scenario: It is Budget day. Going in, most economists on Dalal Street had pencilled in gross market borrowing of about 14.5 lakh crore rupees for the coming year. The Finance Minister's Budget documents show gross borrowing of 15.2 lakh crore rupees, about 70,000 crore higher than the street estimate, even though the fiscal deficit target itself came in roughly in line with expectations.
body.prompt: What is the most likely immediate reaction in the bond market, and which set of stocks would you expect to underperform in the first hour of trade?
body.modelAnswer: A higher than expected borrowing number means more bond supply than the market had priced in, so 10-year G-Sec yields typically rise (bond prices fall) even though the deficit percentage itself was not a surprise, because the absolute rupee amount of paper hitting the market is what banks and insurers actually have to absorb. PSU banks and NBFCs that carry large government bond portfolios tend to see near-term mark-to-market pressure on their investment books, and this usually shows up as underperformance against the broader Bank Nifty index in the opening hour of trade.

children.text: Capex Versus Welfare Spending: Reading the Composition, Not Just the Total

Two Budgets can show an identical fiscal deficit and still send completely different signals to the market, because what matters just as much as how much the government spends is what it spends on. A rupee spent on capital expenditure, roads, railways, ports, defence hardware, tends to have a larger and longer lasting multiplier effect on GDP than a rupee spent on subsidies or revenue expenditure, because capex creates durable assets and pulls in private investment alongside it.

This is why capex allocation growth has become one of the most closely tracked single line items in recent Budgets. A Budget that pushes capex spending well ahead of nominal GDP growth is read as pro-cyclical for industrials, cement, capital goods and infrastructure financiers. A Budget that leans harder into welfare and subsidy spending instead tends to favour rural consumption names, two-wheelers and FMCG, particularly in the months before a state or general election.

columns.label: Capex-heavy Budget
points: Favours infrastructure, cement, capital goods and PSU banks that finance large projects
Signals a longer investment cycle, usually read positively by FIIs positioning on India's growth story
Shows up first in order books of EPC and infrastructure players, and in steel and cement volumes

columns.label: Consumption-heavy Budget
points: Favours FMCG, two-wheelers and rural-facing consumer names
Common in the Budget preceding a major state or general election
Shows up faster in quarterly volume growth than in capex order books, which take longer to translate into earnings

children.text: Tax Proposals: The Most Direct Line to Your Own Portfolio

Tax changes are the part of the Budget that hits your own return calculations directly, not just the broad market. The FY26 Budget, for instance, raised the nil-tax threshold under the new income tax regime to 12 lakh rupees of taxable income (effectively about 12.75 lakh rupees for salaried taxpayers once the standard deduction is included), putting more disposable income directly into the hands of the urban middle class. That single change was read by the market as a direct tailwind for consumption stocks in the weeks that followed.

body.label: FY26 nil-tax threshold (new regime)
body.context: A direct boost to disposable income, read by the market as supportive for consumption-linked stocks.

body.text: Capital gains tax rates and holding period rules, with exact statutory citations, are covered in full in the dedicated Capital Gains course on this platform. This lesson deliberately keeps tax detail at the level relevant to reading Budget day market reaction, not as a substitute for that detailed treatment.

children.text: Three More Line Items Worth Scanning
Customs duty changes on specific inputs, which can move gems and jewellery, electronics assembly or textile stocks within a single sector even when the broad market is flat
Any change to Securities Transaction Tax (STT), which directly affects trading costs on NSE and BSE and can move broking and exchange stocks
Disinvestment and PSU-specific announcements, which tend to move individual PSU counters more sharply than the index
Reading Budget Day Like a Fund Manager

Retail investors often watch the Budget speech for slogans. Professionals watch it with the Budget documents open in a second window, because the speech is edited for television and the real numbers sit in the fine print. Open your broker app, Zerodha, Groww or whichever you use, in the background, and you will see Nifty and Bank Nifty start reacting within seconds of the borrowing and deficit numbers crossing the wires, often well before the Finance Minister finishes speaking.

body.title: Your Budget Day Checklist
steps: Compare the fiscal deficit target to the street's consensus estimate, not to last year's number
Check the gross and net market borrowing figures against pre-Budget economist estimates
Look at capex allocation growth versus nominal GDP growth to gauge whether this is a pro-cyclical or a cautious Budget
Scan the tax proposals for anything that changes disposable income or capital markets transaction costs
Watch the 10-year G-Sec yield and Bank Nifty in the first 30 minutes of trade on NSE, since bond and bank reactions tend to lead the broader Nifty
Check the disinvestment target and any PSU-specific mentions if you hold PSU exposure

body.title: Deficit Versus Borrowing
body.question: The Budget's fiscal deficit target comes in exactly in line with street estimates, but the gross market borrowing number is meaningfully higher than expected. What is the most likely explanation, and what should a bond investor watch?
options: The government is spending less than expected, so borrowing should be lower, not higher, and this is likely a data error

A higher borrowing number against an unchanged deficit usually means non-borrowing receipts, such as disinvestment or non-tax revenue, are assumed lower than the market expected, so a larger share of the same deficit is funded through debt
Gross borrowing and the fiscal deficit are unrelated figures and this combination has no particular significance
This always means the Budget has moved to off-balance-sheet borrowing, which is not permitted under the FRBM Act
body.explanation: The fiscal deficit is the gap between total expenditure and total receipts excluding borrowing. If that gap is unchanged but gross borrowing is higher, it usually means some other financing source, such as disinvestment proceeds, small savings collections or non-tax revenue, is assumed to be lower than the market expected, so a larger share of the same deficit is being funded through market borrowing instead. A bond investor should watch this closely, because it directly changes the supply of G-Secs hitting the market that year, independent of what the headline deficit number implies.

body.title: Quick Deficit Check
body.prompt: A hypothetical Union Budget shows total receipts (excluding borrowing) of 32 lakh crore rupees and total expenditure of 39 lakh crore rupees. What is the fiscal deficit, in lakh crore rupees?
body.explanation: Fiscal deficit is total expenditure minus total receipts excluding borrowing: 39 minus 32 equals 7 lakh crore rupees. This is the amount the government needs to raise through market borrowing and other financing sources for the year.

body.text: Nothing in this lesson is investment advice. It is educational content on how Budget mechanics tend to move markets, consistent with SEBI's guidelines for registered research analysts on this platform.

points: The Union Budget moves markets through three channels: how much the government borrows, what it spends on, and what it changes in taxation
The fiscal deficit target matters less in isolation than in comparison to the street's consensus estimate going in
Gross market borrowing, not just the deficit percentage, is what the bond market actually has to absorb, and it can move the 10-year G-Sec yield within the hour
Capex-heavy Budgets tend to favour industrials, cement and capital goods, while consumption-heavy Budgets favour FMCG and rural-facing names
Reading the Budget well means comparing every number to what the market expected, not just to what was announced
